questions.q: Name the four main modes of transport used in India to move goods and people.
questions.a: The four modes are road, rail, water, and airway. If a student misses one, they are likely thinking only of what they see daily (like roads) and ignoring the national-scale infrastructure.

questions.q: Why do we describe transport networks as the "arteries" of an economy?
questions.a: They are called arteries because they keep goods and people moving between sectors, just as arteries circulate blood to keep the body functioning. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks transport is just "travel" rather than a vital support system for production and trade.

questions.q: If a village produces tomatoes, how does a road network help the farmer earn more money?
questions.a: A road allows the farmer to transport tomatoes quickly to a larger market before they spoil. A wrong answer shows a lack of understanding of the connection between physical infrastructure and economic value (perishability).

questions.q: Compare the role of a National Highway versus a rural village road.
questions.a: National highways handle large-scale, long-distance traffic between cities, while rural roads connect villages to local markets and schools. A wrong answer indicates the student hasn't differentiated between local connectivity and national integration.

questions.q: Is a cargo ship moving tea from India to another country part of the transport network? Why?
questions.a: Yes, because it is the "waterway" component of the network that facilitates the final step of trade (export). Answering "no" suggests the student thinks transport is only for people or only happens on land.

questions.q: Design a simple plan for a remote mountain village to connect to the nearest town. What mode of transport would you prioritize first and why?
questions.a: A good answer would prioritize a road, as it is the most flexible for short-distance, small-scale transport to reach markets. A poor answer suggests something unrealistic, like building an airport for a small village, showing a lack of practical economic reasoning.
